proposedDescription: Black carpet beetles are small, dark, oval beetles whose young have a very different appearance and appetite. The narrow, brown, hairy larvae carry a long tuft at the rear and feed on wool, fur, feathers and other animal materials. Adults visit flowers for pollen and nectar and may enter buildings to lay eggs. Indoors, larvae can remain hidden in lint, stored textiles or insect collections; shed skins and irregular damage are often easier to find than the beetles themselves.
identification: Look for a dark oval adult about 3–5 mm long, or a tapered brown larva with a long tail tuft. Other carpet beetles require comparison.
actions: Inspect susceptible textiles and stored foods, vacuum accumulated lint and pet hair, and isolate infested items for appropriate cleaning.
researchNotes: Read the Gahlhoff UF/IFAS account and independently authored UC IPM pest notes. Adult longevity differs between accounts; omitted. Penn State and Missouri access failures were replaced by UC IPM.

claims: Adult appearance and flower feeding; larval animal-material diet; inspection and vacuuming.
Species-specific size, dark adult color and contrasting larval form; fabric pest context.

proposedDescription: Black cherry aphids gather on tender cherry growth, where their glossy dark bodies stand out against the leaves. Feeding can curl sweet-cherry leaves tightly around the colony and distort young shoots. The aphids also leave sticky honeydew that can support dark sooty mold. Eggs spend the winter on cherry twigs, while later generations commonly move to plants in the mustard family for summer. Lady beetles, lacewings and other predators help limit their numbers in orchards.
identification: Shiny brown-black to black aphids clustered inside curled cherry leaves; adults may be winged or wingless.
actions: Check new growth around bud break and protect predatory insects. Seek local orchard advice if young trees develop heavy infestations.

sources.title: UC IPM — Cherry Pest Management Guidelines

researchNotes: Read Long and Riedl's WSU account and UC's cherry guidelines, black cherry aphid section, page 12 of PDF. Their separately authored accounts agree on seasonal hosts, curling and predators. Penn State was blocked and not counted.

claims: Glossy appearance, sweet-cherry leaf curling, honeydew, seasonal host shift and monitoring.
Overwintering eggs, mustard summer hosts, damage to young trees and natural enemies.

proposedDescription: Black citrus aphid is a small, dark sap-feeding insect found on soft new growth of citrus and many other plants. Coffee, cacao and ornamental shrubs are among its hosts. Colonies can curl or distort young leaves and deposit sticky honeydew, on which sooty mold grows. Despite its name, it is not restricted to citrus. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps often keep colonies in check, and the importance of this aphid varies with the crop and region.
identification: Dull black adults on tender growth suggest this species, but antenna and wing details distinguish it from similar dark citrus aphids.
actions: Inspect new flushes and preserve natural enemies. Confirm the aphid before deciding whether treatment is warranted.
researchNotes: Both sources use Toxoptera aurantii for the catalog's Aphis aurantii. Name reconciliation is an editorial taxonomic note; retain catalog ID. Hawaii account is authored by Mau and Kessing and is independent of the UF citrus account. Do not confuse with T. citricida or transfer its stronger virus-vector role.

claims: Dull black adults, broad host range, tender-growth feeding, honeydew and biological control.
Coffee, cacao and ornamental hosts; leaf distortion and predators or parasitoids.

proposedDescription: Black henbane is a sticky, unpleasant-smelling member of the nightshade family that grows as an annual or biennial. It occurs along roadsides, fences and disturbed pastures, sometimes forming dense patches. Originally brought to North America for ornamental and medicinal use, it now grows outside cultivation in many areas. Its historical use should not suggest a safe household remedy: every part contains toxic alkaloids. A plant may spend its first season as a low rosette before producing an upright flowering stem.
identification: Look for coarse hairy foliage, a sticky feel and foul odor; use photographs rather than handling or tasting a suspected plant.
actions: Keep children and livestock from eating it. Obtain local identification and removal guidance; avoid bare-skin contact.

sources.title: University of Nevada, Reno — Managing Black Henbane
Montana State — Black Henbane Identification, Biology and Integrated Management

researchNotes: Read Nevada Extension and Pokorny, Mangold and Stoy's Montana account. Regional weed impacts are kept separate from the species' entire range; no medical-use instructions or toxicity dose is supplied.

claims: Annual or biennial habit, rosette, disturbed pasture habitat, odor and toxic alkaloids.
Introduction history, western pasture impacts and toxicity including skin irritation.

proposedDescription: Black imported fire ants live in colonies with conspicuous soil mounds and workers of several sizes. Workers are mostly brownish black, sometimes with a reddish patch on the abdomen, and can deliver a painful sting. Introduced populations are established in parts of the southeastern United States. This species is closely related to the red imported fire ant and can hybridize with it, so color alone is not a reliable way to separate them. Specialist examination may be needed for a firm identification.
identification: Variable-sized dark workers, two waist segments and ten-segmented antennae ending in a two-part club. Hybrid fire ants can look intermediate.
actions: Avoid disturbing mounds or handling ants. Ask local extension or pest specialists to confirm identity and advise on site-specific management.

sources.title: University of Georgia — Managing Imported Fire Ants in Urban Areas

researchNotes: MacGown and Whitehouse's museum diagnosis independently complements Suiter's UGA management account. Group-level management facts are used only where the source explicitly includes S. richteri. Hybrid identification uncertainty is substantive, not a reason to merge IDs.

claims: Worker morphology, variable size, mounds and hybrid identification difficulty.
S. richteri included among introduced southeastern fire ants; stinging hazard.

proposedDescription: Black medick is a low, spreading member of the pea family often seen in lawns, field edges and disturbed ground. Its leaves have three small leaflets, giving it a clover-like appearance, but the central leaflet has a short stalk of its own. Rounded clusters of tiny yellow flowers develop into dark seedpods, which explain the common name. It often grows where turf is thin or soil is poor, and its taproot supports a mat of stems close to the ground.
identification: Three leaflets with fine teeth near their tips, a stalked middle leaflet, yellow flower clusters and black mature pods.
actions: Identify it before removing similar clovers. Small unwanted patches can be pulled; improve thin turf rather than relying on repeated mowing alone.
researchNotes: NC State's institutional account and Hartzler's Iowa State account independently support the overview. Michigan Extension supports hand removal. Life cycle varies geographically, so no universal annual-only claim.

claims: Pea family, trifoliate leaves, low habit, habitat and taproot.
Black pods, yellow flowers, leaf teeth and mat-forming growth.
Small patches can be hand pulled; low habit evades mowing.

proposedDescription: Black mimosa is a prickly, woody shrub with finely divided leaves that fold when touched. Rounded pink to mauve flower heads are followed by clusters of bristly brown pods. It favors wet ground, including floodplains, stream edges and abandoned fields. Native to tropical America, it has become a major wetland invader in northern Australia, where dense stands replace open vegetation and obstruct access. Its sensitive foliage resembles that of smaller sensitive plants, but mature black mimosa forms a substantial shrub.
identification: Prickly woody stems, many paired leaflets, pink rounded flower heads and densely bristly pods distinguish it from low-growing sensitive plants.
actions: Photograph suspect plants without spreading pods or soil. Seek local weed advice before disturbing a wetland infestation.
researchNotes: Read NT government's field guidance and the independently authored Más and Lugo-Torres USDA flora, PDF pages 86–87. Australian impacts are explicitly regional.

sources.title: USDA NRCS — Common Weeds in Puerto Rico and U.S. Virgin Islands

claims: Sensitive leaves, prickles, flowers and Australian wetland impact.
Mimosa pigra morphology, bristly pods and humid floodplain habitat.

proposedDescription: Black mustard is an upright annual with bright yellow flowers and a loose rosette of lower leaves. The lower leaves are lobed, while leaves higher on the stem become narrow and undivided. Its short, slender seedpods stand close against the flowering stem, a useful distinction from several other yellow-flowered mustards. Mature plants can rise well above surrounding low vegetation. The plant is widely known under the name Brassica nigra, although modern taxonomic treatments sometimes place it in another genus.
identification: Check the short four-angled pods held close to the stem, bright yellow petals and contrast between lobed lower and narrow upper leaves.
actions: Photograph mature pods as well as flowers for identification before removing or recording a suspected population.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand supplies morphology. Kew currently treats Brassica nigra as a synonym of Mutarda nigra, not the Rhamphospermum name found elsewhere. Retain catalog ID and flag nomenclature review. Habitat/impact claims omitted rather than inferred from mustard relatives.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand — Brassica nigra

claims: Annual stature, leaves, bright yellow flowers and appressed pods.
Current synonym treatment under Mutarda nigra.

proposedDescription: Black nightshade is a branching herb with small white flowers and clusters of berries that change from green to black or purplish black. It grows in sunny, disturbed places such as fields, gardens and roadsides. Birds can spread its seeds after eating the fruit. Identification deserves care: several closely related nightshades look alike, and New England records have often used this name too broadly. The leaves and unripe fruit contain toxic compounds, so appearance alone is no basis for treating it as food.
identification: Small white flowers with yellow anthers, clustered dark berries and unarmed green or purple-tinged stems; expert comparison is needed within the black-nightshade group.
actions: Do not taste plants to identify them. Submit clear flower, ripe fruit and leaf photographs for taxon confirmation.
researchNotes: NC State supports morphology and ecology; Native Plant Trust explicitly warns that many New England S. nigrum collections are native S. ptycanthum. No universal North American nonnative claim and no edible-fruit recommendation.

sources.title: Native Plant Trust — European Black Nightshade

claims: Morphology, disturbed sunny sites, bird dispersal and toxicity of leaves/unripe berries.
Rare New England introduction and frequent misidentification.

proposedDescription: Black poui, better known in many places as jacaranda, is a South American tree grown for its blue-purple flowers and fine, fern-like foliage. Its spreading branches create light shade, and the flowers can form a colorful carpet beneath the canopy. Rounded, woody seed capsules persist after flowering. It does best in warm conditions with sunshine and well-drained soil; frost limits where it can thrive. Its presence as a planted ornamental should be distinguished from evidence that it has escaped cultivation.
identification: Finely divided leaves, clusters of tubular blue-purple flowers and flattened woody seed capsules are useful combined clues.
actions: Confirm local escape or weed status before choosing it for planting. Have a qualified arborist assess weak branch attachments near paths or buildings.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS species account and RHS species profile are independent horticultural sources. RHS genus paragraph was not used as species-specific evidence; UF supplies detailed morphology. Florida source does not classify it as a problem species in its assessment.

claims: Fernlike canopy, flower and fruit features, South American origin, drainage and structural pruning.
Species is frost tender and suited to well-drained soil in sun.

proposedDescription: Black rats are slender, agile rodents also called roof rats or ship rats. Their long tails help them balance as they climb trees, fences and buildings. They often nest above ground in dense vegetation, attics or wall spaces and forage mainly at night. Fruit and nuts are important foods, but their diet also includes small animals and eggs. Human transport has carried them far beyond their original range, and around buildings they can contaminate food and damage materials by gnawing.
identification: A pointed muzzle, relatively large ears and a tail longer than head and body distinguish adults from stockier Norway rats.
actions: Secure food and waste, close building entry points and seek professional help for established infestations. Keep any traps inaccessible to children and pets.
researchNotes: Read Gillespie's University of Michigan account and UC IPM's independent pest notes. Older ADW habitat generalizations are tempered by UC's acknowledgement that roof rats can also burrow.

claims: Human-mediated distribution, climbing and elevated nesting.
Tail and muzzle identification, nocturnal behavior, diet, damage and exclusion.

proposedDescription: This black scale, also called nigra scale, is a sap-feeding insect found on many tropical and subtropical plants. Adult females look like dark brown or glossy black bumps; they are broader on leaves and often narrower on twigs. Citrus, coffee, mango, avocado, hibiscus and figs are among its hosts. The young crawlers move to new feeding sites, while older stages are usually still. Feeding produces honeydew, and natural enemies can provide substantial control of colonies.
identification: Dark oval to elongated scales up to about 5 mm long; body shape changes with the feeding surface. Confirm against other soft scales.
actions: Inspect leaves and twigs before moving plants. Preserve beneficial insects and obtain a scale identification before treatment.
researchNotes: Read Mau and Kessing's Hawaii account and GIE-FPSO's separately authored INRAE-hosted profile. This is Parasaissetia nigra, not Saissetia oleae despite shared catalog common name. INRAE's historical French lack-of-damage observation is not generalized.

claims: Adult shape and color, crawler dispersal, honeydew and natural control.
Species-specific broad crop and ornamental host range.

proposedDescription: Black scale is a soft scale insect whose mature females resemble dark raised bumps on woody stems. A ridge shaped like the letter H is a particularly useful clue. Young stages settle on leaves and twigs, feeding on plant sap and releasing sticky honeydew. Sooty mold grows on that coating, and heavy colonies can weaken trees. Olive and citrus are familiar hosts, along with many ornamentals. Dense, sheltered foliage can favor the insect, while parasitoid wasps help restrain it.
identification: Brown-black adult females about 5 mm across with an H-shaped back ridge; tiny yellow-orange crawlers require a hand lens.
actions: Monitor honeydew and living scales, preserve natural enemies and use suitable pruning to open dense tree canopies.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS species profile and UC olive IPM guidance independently support the account. Kept distinct from Parasaissetia nigra. Generation counts are omitted because they vary with climate.

sources.title: UC IPM — Black Scale in Olive

claims: Hosts, sap feeding, honeydew, sooty mold and parasitoids.
H-shaped adult ridge, crawler appearance and canopy management.

proposedDescription: Black spiny-tailed iguanas are large lizards with a long tail ringed by sharp scales. Adults are commonly gray or tan with dark bands, while young animals may retain green coloring. They bask in open places and shelter among rocks, walls or burrows. Young iguanas eat many insects; adults take more plant material but still consume animal prey. Native to Mexico and Central America, the species has established populations in Florida, where local wildlife impacts have been documented.
identification: Look for the heavily spined tail and dark crossbands, rather than assuming that a black spiny-tailed iguana is entirely black.
actions: Do not release captive iguanas or attempt to handle large wild ones. In introduced populations, report sightings to local wildlife managers.
researchNotes: UF's McKnight-led Florida synthesis and Tran's independently authored Michigan account support ecology. Florida impact is not extended to its native range; other Ctenosaura require expert comparison.

sources.title: UF/IFAS — Black Spiny-tailed Iguanas on Gasparilla Island

claims: Age-related appearance, spiny tail, diet and Florida populations.
Native range, basking and rocky/open habitat.

proposedDescription: Black sun coral builds branching, tree-like colonies with dark green to black living tissue over a hard pale skeleton. Unlike many familiar reef corals, it lacks the symbiotic algae that supply energy from sunlight. Its polyps capture food carried by the water, and its strong skeleton suits places exposed to currents. Native to the Indo-Pacific, it has also been recorded growing on offshore platforms in the northern Gulf of Mexico. It is a stony coral, despite the name suggesting precious black corals.
identification: Dark branching colonies with projecting tubular polyp cups suggest it; photographs and specialist skeletal comparison are needed to separate similar sun corals.
actions: Record an unexpected colony's location and photographs for marine specialists. Do not collect or move living colonies.
researchNotes: Read original Schuhmacher 1984 reef experiments and Sammarco et al. 2010 Gulf introduction paper: distinct research teams and observations. NEMESIS was an additional synthesis, not counted as an independent duplication of those papers. No extrapolation of T. coccinea impacts.

sources.title: Schuhmacher — Reef-building properties of Tubastraea micranthus
Sammarco et al. — A new coral species introduced into the Atlantic

claims: Lack of algal symbionts, captured food, strong skeleton and current-exposed habitat.
Species identification and Gulf platform introduction; dark tissue and branching form.

proposedDescription: Black swallow-wort is a perennial climbing plant that winds around neighboring vegetation or trails across the ground. Its opposite, oval leaves are glossy green, and its small dark-purple flowers have five triangular lobes. In summer, slender pods develop and later release seeds with silky hairs. The plant comes from southwestern Europe and has established dense patches in parts of North America. Its twining stems and nearly black flowers help distinguish it from the more familiar upright milkweeds.
identification: Opposite pointed leaves, twining stems, tiny dark-purple star-shaped flowers and narrow seedpods; pale swallow-wort has different-colored, longer petals.
actions: Confirm the species and remove small plants with their roots where locally recommended. Prevent mature pods from dispersing during removal.
researchNotes: UConn Wallace, Siegel-Miles and Sowizral field account distinguishes both swallow-worts; only black-specific flower details transferred. Kew independently confirms accepted name and southwestern European range.

claims: Twining habit, leaves, distinct black flowers and seedpods.
Accepted species and native southwestern European range.

proposedDescription: Black thread scale is an armored scale insect with an unusually long, narrow protective cover. Adult females have yellow bodies hidden beneath shiny dark-brown to black covers that look like tiny dashes on a leaf or stem. It feeds on many tropical and subtropical plants, with palms among its common hosts. The yellow young crawlers disperse before settling to feed. Female reproduction does not require mating, and males have not been observed in the accounts used here.
identification: Very slender dark covers about 2–3.5 mm long and roughly eight to ten times as long as wide, with a pale cast skin at one end.
actions: Inspect palms and nursery plants before moving them. Ask an extension specialist to confirm scales and assess living infestations.
researchNotes: UF Espinosa/Hodges/Mannion account and Watson's Diaspididae synthesis have separate authorship, but overlap in cited Miller/Davidson diagnostic literature; this dependency is explicit. Avoid exact host-count claims because compilations differ.

sources.title: Naturalis — Diaspididae of the World: Ischnaspis longirostris

claims: Dimensions, yellow body, crawler color and female reproduction.
Long dark scale cover, terminal cast skin and palm hosts.

proposedDescription: Black twig borer is a tiny beetle that tunnels into small branches of many trees and shrubs. Females make pin-sized entrances, often on the underside of a twig, and establish a chamber where their young develop. Fungi growing inside provide food for the beetles. Leaves beyond an attack may wilt and turn brown, making a dead twig the first obvious sign. Unlike many related ambrosia beetles, it can attack healthy plants as well as stressed ones.
identification: Tiny entrance holes underneath wilting twigs, with a brood chamber inside; adult females are dark beetles roughly 1.5–2 mm long.
actions: Have suspicious twig dieback identified. Prune and appropriately dispose of confirmed infested material, and maintain good plant care.
researchNotes: UF Dixon, Woodruff and Foltz and Hawaii Tenbrink/Hara updated by Wright/Patterson are distinct extension teams. Shared older literature is acknowledged; Hawaii adds regional crop context.

claims: Small adult females, twig galleries, fungal food, dieback and pruning.
Broad woody plant host range and regional establishment.

proposedDescription: Black vine weevil is a dark, broad-snouted beetle that feeds at night and hides by day. Adults leave rounded notches around leaf edges, but the more serious damage usually happens below ground. Its pale, legless grubs eat roots and can cause container plants to wilt or die. Many ornamental plants and some fruits are hosts. Adults cannot fly, yet they climb well, and movement of infested plants can make this a persistent nursery and garden problem.
identification: Dull black, broad-snouted adults with pale yellowish flecks; white C-shaped, brown-headed, legless grubs among roots.
actions: Inspect notched plants and root balls, especially in pots. Hand-collect adults after dark where practical and seek advice for damaging larval infestations.
researchNotes: RHS advice team and Minnesota diagnostic guide independently describe this species. Adult measurements disagree, so the overview omits a universal size. Similar notching by other weevils does not establish identity.

sources.title: University of Minnesota — Black Vine Weevil

claims: Nocturnal flightless adults, grub morphology, container damage and hand collection.
Leaf notches, root feeding, plant decline and adult markings.

proposedDescription: Black wattle is an Australian shrub or tree with finely divided leaves and rounded clusters of pale-yellow or cream flowers. The foliage gives the canopy a soft, feathery appearance, while its seedpods are narrow and often pinched between the seeds. In its native southeastern Australian range it grows in forest, woodland and coastal scrub, including creek banks and hillsides. It has been widely cultivated for tannin and timber products, so a planted tree does not by itself establish a local invasion.
identification: Many tiny paired leaflets, pale rounded flower heads, hairy young branchlets and glands along the leaf axis; compare other feather-leaved wattles.
actions: Record leaves, pods and the planting context before assigning identity or local status. Check regional advice before planting or spreading seed.
researchNotes: Kodela's NSW flora and Brenan's Flora Zambesiaca hosted by Kew are independent descriptions; Kew supplies native-range treatment. No regional invasive impact inferred from global cultivation.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney — Acacia mearnsii

claims: Morphology, Australian habitats and tannin cultivation.
Native southeastern Australia, flowers and pod morphology.

proposedDescription: Blackberry lily is a perennial in the iris family, despite its lily-like common name. Fans of upright, sword-shaped leaves rise from underground stems, and wiry flowering stems carry orange blooms marked with red spots. Later, the seed capsules split open to show shiny black seeds clustered like a blackberry. Native to eastern and southeastern Asia, it is widely grown as an ornamental. The showy black clusters are seeds rather than edible berries, an easy distinction to miss.
identification: Flattened fans of iris-like leaves, six-parted orange flowers with red spots, and opened capsules displaying black seed clusters.
actions: Use flowers and capsules to confirm identification. Do not mistake its seed clusters for fruit intended for eating.
researchNotes: NC State morphology and Denver Botanic Gardens accession profile independently support family, appearance and Asian range. Belamcanda chinensis is the older synonym; retain Iris domestica ID.

claims: Fan leaves, underground rhizome, spotted orange flowers and blackberry-like seed capsules.
Iris family, Asian range, flower colors and Belamcanda synonym.

proposedDescription: Blackeyed susan vine is a twining plant with soft, triangular to heart-shaped leaves and flowers that usually have a dark central eye. Wild forms commonly flower in yellow or orange, while garden selections offer additional colors. Native to tropical and southern Africa and Madagascar, it grows in varied habitats from woodland edges to disturbed vegetation. In gardens its stems climb supports or trail from baskets. It is distinct from the upright North American Rudbeckia flowers that share the black-eyed Susan name.
identification: Twining stems, opposite triangular or heart-shaped leaves, and a tubular flower opening into a broad face with a dark throat.
actions: Confirm the scientific name when buying or reporting it. Keep garden material contained and check local status before planting in warm climates.
researchNotes: Kew's Flora Zambesiaca/Somalia accounts and Illinois horticultural guidance are independent. Growth duration varies with climate; not labeled universally annual or universally invasive.

claims: Native range, twining habit, leaves, flowers and varied habitats.
Garden flower colors, vine habit and use on trellises/baskets.

proposedDescription: Blackwood is an Australian tree with dark, deeply furrowed bark and a leafy crown that can reach forest-tree proportions. Its mature foliage consists of flattened leaf stalks, called phyllodes, with several strong lengthwise veins. Pale cream to yellow flower balls are followed by twisting brown pods; each dark seed is partly surrounded by a bright orange or reddish thread. In its native range it grows in moist forests, including wet eucalyptus forest and cooler rainforest.
identification: Look for long, narrow leaflike phyllodes with three to five prominent veins, pale round flower heads, twisted pods and dark fissured bark.
actions: Photograph foliage, pods and the whole tree for confirmation. Check regional planting guidance before choosing it for a garden.
researchNotes: NSW Flora supplies morphology and native habitat; Kew independently confirms accepted name and eastern/southeastern Australian native range. Regional introduction does not establish invasive behavior everywhere.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Acacia melanoxylon

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney / NSW Flora
claims: Tree height, phyllode veins, pale flower heads, twisted pods, colored seed funicle and wet forest habitat.
Accepted species; native eastern and southeastern Australia; woody growth.

proposedDescription: The plant catalogued here as bladder campion is Silene latifolia, usually called white campion. This short-lived perennial has soft, hairy leaves in opposite pairs and white flowers with five deeply notched petals. Behind each flower is a swollen, veined green cup. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Native to Europe and introduced in North America, it grows in fields, meadows and disturbed ground. It can hybridize with red campion, producing plants with pink flowers.
identification: Look for hairy opposite leaves, five split white petals and a veined swollen flower cup. Separate male and female plants and the hairy foliage help distinguish it from true bladder campion.
actions: Confirm the scientific name before recording or removing plants; include close photographs of the flower cup, leaves and stems.
researchNotes: Catalog common-name mismatch: Silene latifolia is white campion; bladder campion normally refers to S. vulgaris. Keep this ID distinct. Missouri treatment concerns S. latifolia subsp. alba; used only for shared practical morphology. Go Botany independently supports species ecology and hybridization.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: White campion, European origin, disturbed habitats and hybridization with S. dioica.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Pamela Borden Trewatha / Missouri State University
claims: Hairy opposite leaves, notched petals, veined calyx, separate sexes and comparison with bladder campion.

proposedDescription: Blessed milkthistle is a large annual or biennial thistle whose glossy green leaves are boldly marbled with white. Sharp spines line the leaves and the broad bracts surrounding its pink-purple flower heads. Young plants begin as ground-level rosettes before sending up tall flowering stems. Originally from southern Europe, it has been cultivated as an herb and can escape into disturbed ground and pasture. Its conspicuous foliage helps separate it from many other thistles even before it flowers.
identification: Look for shiny, white-marbled leaves with spiny edges and large purple heads surrounded by broad, projecting spiny bracts.
actions: Wear protective clothing when handling confirmed plants. Where removal is appropriate, dig small plants before seed develops and contain seed heads; avoid spreading seeds by mowing mature stands.
researchNotes: Regional weed advice comes from King County; no current legal designation generalized nationwide. Herbal cultivation is historical context, not a claim of medical benefit.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: Southern European origin, herbal cultivation and occasional New England escapes.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: King County Noxious Weed Control Program
claims: White leaf marbling, spiny leaves/bracts, annual or biennial habit, pasture habitat and seed containment.

proposedDescription: Blindeyes, also called long-headed or field poppy, is a slender annual with hairy stems, divided leaves and delicate orange-red flowers. Its four petals may have little or no dark marking at their bases. The fruit is especially useful for recognition: a smooth, elongated capsule rather than the short, rounded capsule of some other poppies. Fine hairs lie flat against the upper flower stalk. A taproot anchors the plant, while its dry capsules release many small seeds.
identification: Check the elongated, club-shaped capsule and the flattened hairs near the top of the flower stalk; flower color alone is unreliable.
actions: Photograph mature capsules and flower-stalk hairs before assigning the species. Prevent movement of seed-bearing material where control is locally recommended.
researchNotes: The catalog common name Blindeyes is retained; sources also use field poppy. Identification relies on species-level flora characters rather than a generic red-poppy appearance.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Papaver dubium

claims: Annual habit, dissected leaves, petal markings, appressed upper stalk hairs and elongated capsule.
Hairy erect stems, divided leaves, orange-red flowers, taproot and many-seeded capsules.

proposedDescription: Blood red tassel flower is a tropical shrub or small tree grown for round, bright red flower clusters that resemble powder puffs. The showy threads are the flowers' long stamens. Its leaves are twice divided into small leaflets, giving the spreading crown a fine texture. Firm brown pods follow the flowers. Kew places its native range in Bolivia, while cultivated plants are familiar in warm gardens, where moist, well-drained soil and sun or partial shade suit its growth.
identification: Look for red powder-puff flower heads and twice-divided leaves with one pair of main leaflet-bearing branches. Check pods and leaves as well as flowers.
actions: Use photographs of flowers, leaf structure and pods to confirm the plant. Check local planting guidance before introducing it to a new garden.
researchNotes: Native-range disagreement: NParks lists Borneo and Bolivia, whereas Kew WCVP lists Bolivia. Follow Kew for range and NParks for horticultural morphology; do not repeat Borneo as established native range.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Calliandra haematocephala

claims: Shrub/tree habit, bipinnate leaves, red stamens, dry pods and cultivation conditions.
Accepted name; native Bolivia; shrub or tree of seasonally dry tropical regions.

proposedDescription: Bloodflower is a tropical milkweed with narrow, opposite leaves and clusters of red-orange flowers topped by yellow or orange crowns. Its upright stems release milky sap when damaged, and slender pods eventually open to release silky-haired seeds. It stays leafy in warm conditions but is often grown as an annual where winters are cold. Monarch caterpillars feed on it, yet persistent winter growth in warm regions can encourage parasite buildup, making locally native milkweeds a better garden choice there.
identification: Look for opposite narrow leaves, milky sap and red-orange flowers with raised yellow crowns; pods contain seeds attached to silky hairs.
actions: Choose milkweeds appropriate to your region and follow local monarch guidance. Avoid contact with the sap and keep plant material away from children and pets.
researchNotes: Regional overwintering concern is supported by Wisconsin Extension; do not imply all milkweed planting is harmful. No medicinal or edible-use claims.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
claims: Flower colors and clusters, narrow foliage, seed pods and irritating/toxic sap.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Susan Mahr / University of Wisconsin Extension
claims: Frost-tender perennial habit, monarch host relationship, winter parasite concern and native milkweed alternatives.

proposedDescription: Bloody geranium is a low, spreading perennial often grown in gardens for its magenta-pink flowers. Each flower has five broad petals marked with darker veins, while the leaves are deeply divided into narrow, fingerlike lobes. Underground stems allow a clump to widen over time. Native to Europe and western Asia, it favors well-drained ground in sun or partial shade. Garden escapes have been documented in parts of North America, including disturbed sites and meadows in New England.
identification: Look for low clumps, deeply cut palm-shaped leaves and five-petaled pink-magenta flowers with darker veins. Cultivars can differ in flower color.
actions: Confirm garden escapes with photographs of leaves, flowers and growth habit. Keep unwanted spreading clumps within the intended planting area.
researchNotes: RHS provides horticultural morphology; Native Plant Trust independently documents regional escapes. This is a hardy Geranium species, not a bedding Pelargonium.

claims: Low rhizomatous perennial, narrow leaf lobes, veined magenta flowers and well-drained habitat preference.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Native Plant Trust / Flora Novae Angliae
claims: European/western Asian origin, garden cultivation and occasional New England escapes.

proposedDescription: Bloody red shrimp is a tiny freshwater crustacean with prominent black eyes and a partly transparent body speckled red or orange. Its color changes with light and temperature, so some individuals look almost colorless. Swarms shelter around rocks, docks and other shaded structures, emerging to feed on small aquatic organisms. Native to the Ponto-Caspian region, it has spread to the Great Lakes. Its flat-ended tail, with a long spine at each corner, is more useful for identification than redness alone.
identification: Use magnification to check the flat-ended tail and two corner spines; the native Great Lakes Mysis diluviana has a forked tail.
actions: Photograph suspected sightings and record the location. Clean, drain and dry boats and gear before moving between waters; never move live bait or water to another site.
researchNotes: Pennsylvania Sea Grant and Fisheries and Oceans Canada are separate institutional treatments. Great Lakes impacts remain uncertain; avoid turning potential food-web effects into established declines.

claims: Variable red pigmentation, stalked eyes, flat telson, hard sheltered habitat and prevention.
Swarms, feeding, comparison with Mysis diluviana, Great Lakes introduction and clean-drain-dry advice.

proposedDescription: This blow fly is often called the hairy maggot blow fly because its older larvae carry fleshy, spiny projections that give them a bristly appearance. Adults are metallic green with a bluish sheen and resemble several other blow flies. The larvae develop in animal remains, where older stages may also prey on other maggots. The species is important in forensic research and livestock health; in some regions it can infest existing animal wounds as well as carrion.
identification: Metallic adults need specialist examination. Older larvae have conspicuous fleshy projections, but similar Chrysomya species mean a photograph may not settle identification.
actions: Avoid handling animal remains to obtain specimens. Ask an entomologist to confirm suspected flies, and seek veterinary help for a live animal with a maggot-infested wound.
researchNotes: UF authored account and the Australian carrion-fly identification treatment are distinct syntheses, though both cite some shared research, including Baumgartner. No current distribution inferred from older records.

sources.title: Hairy maggot blow fly: Chrysomya rufifacies

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of Florida IFAS / Featured Creatures
claims: Metallic adult appearance, spiny larval tubercles, carrion feeding, predation and livestock associations.
Secondary carrion association, predatory older larvae, spiny skin and forensic importance.

proposedDescription: Blue alfalfa aphid is a soft-bodied, blue-green insect that feeds on alfalfa and other legumes. Long legs, antennae and paired rear tubes give it a slender appearance. Colonies often gather on young shoots and stems, especially in cool weather. Feeding can stunt plants, while sticky honeydew supports dark sooty mold. It closely resembles the pea aphid and may occur alongside it, but its antennae darken gradually toward the tips instead of carrying distinct dark bands at the joints.
identification: Examine the antennae with magnification: gradual darkening toward the tip supports blue alfalfa aphid; dark bands on each segment suggest pea aphid.
actions: Confirm the aphid species and monitor natural enemies as well as aphid numbers. Use locally recommended resistant alfalfa varieties and crop-specific monitoring guidance.
researchNotes: UC alfalfa specialists and Cesar Australia/SARDI provide independently authored crop guidance. Regional seasons and treatment thresholds are not generalized nationally.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of California Statewide IPM / alfalfa specialists
claims: Antennal distinction, shoot feeding, cool-season activity, growth damage and natural-enemy conservation.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Cesar Australia and South Australian Research and Development Institute
claims: Blue-green appearance, legume hosts, long appendages and plant damage.

proposedDescription: Blue fieldmadder is a small annual that can spread into a low, rough-textured mat. Narrow leaves and leaflike structures form rings around its square stems, making it resemble a miniature bedstraw. The tiny flowers set it apart: they are pinkish mauve, with a short tube opening into four spreading lobes, clustered near stem tips. Native across parts of Europe, North Africa and Asia, it also grows beyond that range in fields, grassland and other open, disturbed places.
identification: Look for square, rough stems, rings of narrow leaves and tiny mauve-pink flowers with four lobes. It is easily overlooked among small bedstraws.
actions: Take close photographs of flowers and leaf rings for confirmation. Remove unwanted plants before seed develops where local weed guidance recommends it.
researchNotes: Oxford botanical account and New Zealand flora are independent treatments. Catalog blue name does not imply consistently blue flowers; flora describes mauve, occasionally white.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Sherardia arvensis

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New Zealand Flora / Webb and colleagues
claims: Annual mat-forming habit, square rough stems and small mauve four-lobed flowers.
Bedstraw comparison, terminal flower clusters, native range and open-ground habitats.

proposedDescription: Blue gum galling wasp is a small insect whose larvae develop inside swollen growths on blue gum eucalyptus. The damaged shoots can look distorted and discolored, making the galls easier to notice than the adult wasps. The species was described scientifically in 2009 after infestations were found in Los Angeles County, California. Published accounts associate it with the blue gum complex; unusual eucalyptus galls on their own do not prove that this particular wasp is present.
identification: Look for abnormal swellings and distorted shoots on blue gum eucalyptus. Confirm the insect through an entomologist; gall shape alone is insufficient.
actions: Photograph the affected shoots and host tree, record the location and contact a local plant diagnostic service. Avoid moving affected nursery plants or cut branches.
researchNotes: Hoddle's UCR account and La Salle, Arakelian, Garrison and Gates' taxonomic paper are separately authored; Arakelian supplies UCR photographs and overlaps in discovery lineage. Paper abstract supports species, host and California introduction only. Historical forecasts of spread are omitted.

sources.title: A new species of invasive gall wasp on blue gum in California

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Mark Hoddle / University of California Riverside
claims: Internal gall-feeding larvae, distorted blue gum shoots and Los Angeles discovery.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: John La Salle, Gevork Arakelian, Rosser Garrison and Michael Gates / 2009 taxonomic study
claims: Species described in 2009 as gall inducer of Eucalyptus globulus in California.

proposedDescription: Blue panicum is a tall, coarse perennial grass that grows in dense clumps and spreads by short underground stems. Its sturdy stems have conspicuous joints, while the long leaves show a strong middle vein and often wavy margins. Loose, branching seed heads become drooping as they mature. Native to Asia and planted as a forage grass elsewhere, it can escape into open or disturbed ground. Texas records describe it in fields and other open sites, especially on clay loam soils.
identification: Look for large stem joints, broad leaves with a strong midrib, short rhizomes and open seed heads that droop with maturity.
actions: Confirm identification before treating a stand. Seek local livestock or agricultural advice before using it as forage, since growth stage can affect its safety.
researchNotes: Texas A&M and NSW flora are independent regional treatments. Catalog Panicum antidotale retained; no unverified genus reassignment or universal invasive status asserted.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Texas A&M AgriLife / range plant treatment
claims: Coarse perennial clumps, rhizomes, wavy leaves, drooping panicle, introduced forage and Texas habitat.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: S. W. L. Jacobs and C. A. Wall / NSW Flora
claims: Rhizomatous perennial, open panicle, Asian origin and escape from fodder cultivation.

proposedDescription: Blue rattlesnake is a bushy tropical legume, also known as blue rattlepod. Unlike many relatives with divided leaves, it has broad, simple leaves on angular, branching stems. The pea-shaped flowers are pale blue, lavender or whitish, with a darker keel, and are followed by short, inflated, softly hairy pods. Kew places its native range from tropical and subtropical Asia to northern Australia. Elsewhere in the tropics it occurs in open places, including pastures and sandy roadsides.
identification: Look for broad simple leaves, four-angled stems, bluish pea flowers and hairy, inflated pods. Check mature pods to distinguish similar Crotalaria.
actions: Confirm plants using flowers and pods before recording them. Avoid distributing seed-bearing material where the species is unwanted.
researchNotes: Kew hosts separately attributed floras; morphology/habitat here comes from Proctor's Cayman treatment and Gillett/Polhill/Verdcourt, while JCB supplies independently compiled Eastern Ghats occurrence. Catalog common name retained.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Crotalaria verrucosa
Digital Flora of Eastern Ghats: Crotalaria verrucosa

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Kew WCVP; Gillett, Polhill and Verdcourt; George Proctor flora treatments
claims: Native range, annual bushy habit, angular stems, simple leaves, pale flowers, pods and open habitats.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Sankara Rao, Arun Singh, Deepak Kumar, Raja Swamy and Navendu Page / IISc
claims: Species identity and documented Eastern Ghats localities from regional floras.

proposedDescription: The fungus catalogued as Ophiostoma tenellum is now called Jamesreidia tenella. It is a microscopic wood-associated fungus recorded from North America, including collections connected with bark beetles in spruce logs. It has also been isolated from logs used to grow shiitake mushrooms, where it can interfere with mushroom growth. The catalog label blue stain describes a broad type of wood discoloration, not a reliable species diagnosis. Identifying this fungus requires examination of its microscopic structures and, when needed, DNA evidence.
identification: Wood discoloration alone cannot identify this species. A fungal laboratory must compare microscopic features and current taxonomic references.
actions: For suspicious timber or mushroom-production logs, seek a plant-pathology or mycology laboratory diagnosis before selecting a response.
researchNotes: Important reassignment: Ophiostoma tenellum = Ceratocystis tenella = Jamesreidia tenella (de Beer et al. 2022). EFSA's broad blue-stain statement is genus-level and was not converted into a species-specific visual claim. Its listed Microascales/Ceratocystidaceae placement conflicts with the primary Ophiostomatales revision; do not propagate it. North American records do not establish introduced status.

sources.title: Generic boundaries in the Ophiostomatales reconsidered and revised
Commodity risk assessment of maple veneer sheets from Canada, Appendix A.1.1.8

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Z. W. de Beer, M. Procter, M. Wingfield, S. Marincowitz and T. Duong / 2022 revision
claims: Jamesreidia tenella is type of newly delimited Jamesreidia; molecular and morphological taxonomic framework.
Synonyms, North American records, bark-beetle/spruce-log isolation and interference with shiitake growth.

proposedDescription: Blue tilapia is a deep-bodied freshwater fish with a small mouth and an olive to bluish-gray back. Its tail usually has irregular markings and a pink-red outer edge; young fish show a dark spot near the rear of the dorsal fin. It occupies varied waters, from canals and vegetated lakes to rivers and springs. Females shelter eggs and young in their mouths. Introduced populations occur in Florida, where similar tilapias make careful identification important.
identification: Check the deep compressed body, small mouth, irregular tail bands and pink-red tail edge. Similar tilapias and hybrids may require expert confirmation.
actions: Do not release aquarium or aquaculture fish into natural waters. Record clear side and fin photographs and follow local fisheries guidance.
researchNotes: Florida Museum provides specimen-based morphology; USFWS compiles independent ecological literature including Tarkan and Trewavas. No generalized current legal or nationwide establishment claim.

sources.title: Blue Tilapia Ecological Risk Screening Summary

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Museum of Natural History / ichthyology collection
claims: Body and fin markings, juvenile spot, habitats and nonindigenous Florida status.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: US Fish and Wildlife Service synthesis; ecological literature including Tarkan
claims: Female mouthbrooding, varied feeding ecology and introduction pathways.

proposedDescription: Bluebell creeper is an evergreen climbing shrub from Western Australia, with slender twining stems and narrow green leaves. Small, nodding blue flowers hang in clusters and are followed by elongated purple fruits. It is grown ornamentally in mild climates and can climb through nearby vegetation. The name needs care: the similar Billardiera fusiformis is also sold and described as bluebell creeper. Older accounts under Sollya heterophylla may include both species, so identification should use a modern botanical treatment.
identification: Look for narrow leaves, nodding blue flowers and cylindrical purple fruits. Seek expert confirmation where Billardiera fusiformis or horticultural hybrids are possible.
actions: Check the identity and regional planting guidance before purchasing or spreading it. Keep fruiting garden material out of natural vegetation.
researchNotes: ANPSA explicitly discusses B. heterophylla/B. fusiformis confusion and historical Sollya usage; RHS independently describes horticultural appearance. Older broad distribution/weed reports are not silently assigned to this narrower species.

claims: Evergreen climbing habit, narrow leaves, nodding blue flowers, cylindrical purple fruit and Western Australian origin.
Similar species share the common name; historical Sollya taxonomy and horticultural confusion.

proposedDescription: Bluecrown passionflower is a vigorous climbing vine from South America. Tendrils help it grip supports, while deeply lobed leaves surround striking white flowers with a ring of blue, white and dark purple threads. Raised reproductive parts stand above the flower's center. Oval fruits ripen from green to yellow-orange. The vine remains leafy in warm winters but may lose its leaves in colder conditions. It is widely grown on fences and trellises in sunny, well-drained places.
identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves, coiling tendrils and white flowers with a blue-and-white filament ring. Orange oval fruits provide another useful clue.
actions: Keep garden growth within its intended area and check regional advice before planting. Do not infer that leaves or fruits are safe to consume from the common name.
researchNotes: NC State supplies species morphology and native origin; the separately produced RHS Plants/Crocus horticultural entry corroborates leaves, flowers, fruit and growth. No genus-level hardiness claim applied indiscriminately.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
claims: South American vine, tendrils, flower structure, fruit color and climate-dependent foliage.
Deeply lobed glossy leaves, white blue-purple flowers, orange-yellow fruit and vigorous climbing growth.

proposedDescription: Bluegreen saltbush, often called old man saltbush, is a large Australian shrub with silvery-gray foliage. Tiny scales give the leaves their pale appearance; leaf shapes can vary from oval to nearly round even on one plant. Male and female flowers usually grow on separate shrubs, and the developing seeds are enclosed by enlarged, leaflike bracts. It naturally occupies inland dry country, often on heavy soils near floodways, and tolerates both drought and occasional flooding.
identification: Look for a tall gray-silver shrub with scaly, broad leaves and small seeds enclosed by paired fanlike bracts. Leaf shape alone varies too much for certainty.
actions: Use fruiting bracts as well as foliage for identification. Check local suitability before planting; its native Australian habitat should not be treated as an invasive occurrence.
researchNotes: S. W. L. Jacobs' NSW flora and Catherine Viney's ANBG account are independent authorships, with shared regional background references acknowledged.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: S. W. L. Jacobs / NSW Flora
claims: Large perennial shrub, variable broad leaves, separate sexes, fruiting bracts and heavy-soil floodway habitat.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Catherine Viney / Australian National Botanic Gardens
claims: Scaly silvery foliage, variable leaf shape, fruit bracts and drought/flood tolerance.

proposedDescription: Bluemink is the familiar garden ageratum, a small annual grown for clusters of soft-looking flowers. The heads are usually blue or lavender, though cultivated forms may be pink or white. Its broad, softly hairy leaves have shallowly toothed edges, and the stems can be green or reddish. Native to Central America, it favors sunny or partly shaded, well-drained sites. It sometimes escapes cultivation, but North Carolina's flora notes that many records there represent planted specimens rather than wild populations.
identification: Look for clustered fluffy flower heads and broad hairy leaves with rounded teeth. Garden cultivars vary in height and flower color.
actions: Record whether plants are cultivated or growing independently. Photograph leaves and flower heads before distinguishing this species from other Ageratum.
researchNotes: NCSU horticultural account and NC Parks flora inventory are separately maintained sources. Leaf arrangement wording in NCSU is internally inconsistent, so no rigid arrangement claim used. Cultivation records are not treated as establishment.

sources.title: Vascular Plants of North Carolina: Floss-flower

evidence.independentSourceGroup: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
claims: Annual habit, Central American origin, fluffy blue/pink/white heads and hairy toothed foliage.
Many records are cultivated; escapes are uncommon in North Carolina.

proposedDescription: The bluish borer beetle is a metallic wood-boring beetle whose adults vary from blue to green. Native to Eurasia, it is established in parts of North America. Larvae develop in woody stems of honeysuckles; a confirmed Oregon discovery involved damaged twinberry shrubs and beetles emerging from their branches. Its appearance can resemble other Agrilus beetles, so color alone is unreliable. Published assessments describe limited overall economic impact, even though individual ornamental shrubs can suffer noticeable damage.
identification: Photograph the adult, damaged stems and exit holes on the host plant. Blue or green color and a honeysuckle association are clues; a specialist must confirm the species.
actions: Seek entomological confirmation before attributing damage. For confirmed infestations, local specialists can advise removal and disposal of damaged stems.
researchNotes: Gap resolved with the eight-page primary paper by Westcott, Williams and Grotta (2019). That study restricts confirmed North American larval hosts to honeysuckles; adults collected on snowberry do not establish it as a larval host. BugGuide's taxonomic synthesis draws on Jendek and Grebennikov (2009), independently of the Oregon field observations. The genome paper's broader host list was not used.

sources.title: Westcott, Williams & Grotta (2019): Agrilus cyanescens discovered in Oregon

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Westcott, Williams and Grotta (2019), primary Oregon research
claims: Confirmed emergence from Lonicera involucrata; blue-green adults; Eurasian origin; larval host caveats, limited broad impact, damaged-stem disposal.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: BugGuide editors / Jendek and Grebennikov (2009) taxonomy
claims: Agrilus wood-borer classification and taxonomic identification context; broad host list not repeated.

proposedDescription: Boatlily is a tropical perennial that forms clumps of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, usually green above and purple underneath. Its small white flowers sit inside pairs of folded purple bracts that resemble little boats, explaining several of its common names. Short, thick stems keep the leaf rosettes close to the ground. Often grown as a houseplant or warm-climate groundcover, it can spread beyond gardens in suitable climates. The sap may irritate skin, so handling deserves care.
identification: Look for tight rosettes of long, pointed leaves with purple undersides and tiny three-petaled white flowers tucked inside boat-shaped bracts.
actions: Wear gloves when handling or dividing plants. Keep discarded plants and fragments contained, and check regional planting advice before using it outdoors.
researchNotes: NC State and Gilman/UF horticultural treatment are independent sources. Historical names Rhoeo spathacea and R. discolor refer to this taxon. Cultivars may have striped leaves.

sources.title: Tradescantia spathacea: Oyster Plant, Moses in the Cradle

evidence.independentSourceGroup: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
claims: Leaf rosettes, purple undersides, succulent stems, boat-shaped bracts and sap irritation.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of Florida IFAS horticultural extension
claims: Clumping perennial habit, stiff leaves, concealed white flowers and landscape use.

proposedDescription: Bodhi tree is a large fig tree recognized by heart-shaped leaves that taper into unusually long, narrow tips. Its small figs grow near the leaf bases and turn purple to black when ripe. Native to parts of South Asia, it is widely cultivated and holds religious importance in Buddhism and Hinduism. The tree may begin life on another tree before roots reach the ground. In Singapore, birds and small mammals eat its fruits and help disperse the seeds.
identification: Look for heart-shaped leaves with very long tapering tips, gray bark and small paired figs at leaf bases. Damaged parts release white sap.
actions: Confirm young trees before deciding on removal, and use professional arboricultural advice for large established trees. Check local planting guidance and allow adequate space.
researchNotes: NParks supplies morphology, cultural context and Singapore dispersal observations; Kew independently supplies accepted taxonomy and native range. No universal invasive designation or medicinal claims.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Ficus religiosa

claims: Long leaf tips, small purple-black figs, strangler habit, religious significance and animal dispersal in Singapore.
Accepted tree species and South Asian native range.

proposedDescription: Bog bulrush is a wetland sedge with upright, spongy stems that are distinctly three-sided. Its leaves are reduced largely to brown sheaths around the stem bases, so the green stems do most of the visible work. Clusters of small, cone-shaped flower spikelets produce dark brown seeds. It grows in waterlogged ground and wetlands, with a broad native range across the Old World and Australia. The names Scirpus mucronatus and Schoenoplectus mucronatus appear in older accounts of the same species.
identification: Check the three-angled stems with slightly hollowed sides, bladeless basal sheaths and clustered brown spikelets. Mature fruits help separate similar sedges.
actions: Photograph stem cross-section, basal sheaths and mature seed heads. Avoid moving wetland plants or mud between sites, and confirm identity before removal.
researchNotes: NParks lists panglobal native distribution, while Kew distinguishes Old World/Australian native range from introductions; follow Kew for biogeography. NParks perennial and Kew annual/helophyte wording differ, so fixed lifespan omitted.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Schoenoplectiella mucronata

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Singapore National Parks Board / Yong and colleagues 2010
claims: Three-sided spongy stems, bladeless sheaths, clustered spikelets and waterlogged habitat.
Accepted name, Scirpus/Schoenoplectus synonyms and native versus introduced distribution.

proposedDescription: Bolivian fuchsia is a large shrub or small tree from the Andes of Peru, Bolivia and northwestern Argentina. Long clusters of narrow, hanging flowers end its arching branches, usually combining scarlet tubes and petals. Broad leaves have hairy red stalks, and elongated berries darken to purple or nearly black. It is cultivated for its abundant flowers in mild, moist conditions. Some garden forms have white flower tubes with red petals, so flower color alone does not define the species.
identification: Look for arching branches, long dangling tubular flowers, hairy reddish leaf stalks and elongated dark berries. White-tubed garden forms also occur.
actions: Check regional planting advice, especially in mild climates where it can escape. Photograph leaves, flowers and fruit for confirmation.
researchNotes: MNHN horticultural account and Kew WCVP are independent. Native range is broader than Bolivia; regional invasiveness mentioned by MNHN for Réunion is not generalized.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Fuchsia boliviana

claims: Shrub habit, hairy red petioles, pendant scarlet flowers, dark berries and white-tubed cultivar.
Accepted name, shrub/tree habit and native Peru–Bolivia–northwestern Argentina range.

proposedDescription: Bondar's nesting whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect that leaves circular white wax deposits on foliage. Adults are about a millimeter long, with gray-brown wing bands that form an X when viewed from above. Young stages produce fine wax threads and a skirtlike fringe, eventually sitting inside a white waxy nest. Heavy infestations can coat leaves with honeydew and dark sooty mold. It has been recorded on several tropical crops and ornamentals, but related nesting whiteflies can be difficult to distinguish.
identification: Look for X-shaped adult wing markings and circular white wax nests, often contrasting with black sooty mold. Reliable separation from relatives requires microscopic examination.
actions: Photograph leaf undersides and adult wings and consult an extension or diagnostic service. Inspect new plants and avoid moving infested material.
researchNotes: UF diagnostic guide and Munguti et al. Kenya molecular study are independent authorships. Kenya paper detects adults on cassava but cautions that full colonization was not demonstrated; no cassava-virus transmission claim transferred from Bemisia.

sources.title: Pest Identification Guide: Bondar's Nesting Whitefly
Distribution and Molecular Diversity of Whitefly Species Colonizing Cassava in Kenya

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Nicole Casuso and Hugh Smith / University of Florida IFAS
claims: Adult X bands, wax nests and skirts, honeydew/sooty mold, host range and diagnostic limits.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florence Munguti, Dora Kilalo, Evans Nyaboga, Everlyne Wosula, Isaac Macharia and Agnes Mwango'mbe

proposedDescription: Boneseed is a woody South African shrub with yellow daisy-like flowers and small fruits that turn black when ripe. The name usually refers to Chrysanthemoides monilifera subspecies monilifera, whose leathery leaves have toothed edges and whose dry seeds are pale and bone-colored. The broader species also includes bitou bush, a more spreading form with rounder, smoother-edged leaves. Introduced boneseed can form dense stands in parts of Australia and New Zealand, so the subspecies matters when describing its appearance and local behavior.
identification: For boneseed, look for upright branches, toothed leaves, yellow flower heads and pale round seeds. Bitou bush has rounder leaves, more spreading growth and differently shaped seeds.
actions: Confirm the subspecies and consult local weed guidance. Contain ripe fruits during any authorized removal and revisit the site for seedlings.
researchNotes: Catalog is species-level, while common name points to subsp. monilifera. Draft explicitly distinguishes bitou subsp. rotundata; NZ flora treatment chiefly represents boneseed. Chrysanthemoides retained to match catalog; no silent merge.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Chrysanthemoides monilifera

claims: Woody shrub, leathery toothed leaves, yellow heads and black drupes; naturalized boneseed taxon.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries
claims: Boneseed subspecies, pale seeds, comparison with bitou bush and regional weed guidance.

proposedDescription: Bonpland's croton is a branching, partly woody plant with narrow, pointed leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers. The leaves have blunt teeth along their edges. Male and female flowers share the same flowering stem, and the rounded, three-lobed fruit separates into single-seeded sections when ripe. Native to southern South America, it has spread into many tropical regions. In India's Eastern Ghats it is naturalized in disturbed places, including clearings, village margins and fallow ground.
identification: Look for a low, basally branching shrub with narrow toothed leaves, terminal flower clusters and three-lobed capsules. Close flower and fruit photographs are useful.
actions: Confirm identification before recording or removing it. Where unwanted, avoid moving ripe capsules or contaminated soil to new sites.
researchNotes: Kew provides accepted taxonomy/native range; IISc Eastern Ghats flora provides independently compiled morphology and regional naturalization. Avoid confusing this true Croton with ornamental Codiaeum often sold as croton.

sources.title: Plants of the World Online: Croton bonplandianus
Digital Flora of Eastern Ghats: Croton bonplandianus

claims: Accepted subshrub/shrub with southern South American native range.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Sankara Rao and colleagues / Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB
